'''''Nymphaea alba'''''{{snd}}[[common name|commonly called]] the '''white water lily''', '''European white water lily''', or '''white nenuphar''' ({{IPAc-en|"|n|ɛ|n|j|ʊ|f|ɑːr}} {{respell|NEN|yuu|far}}){{snd}}is an [[aquatic plant|aquatic]] [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Nymphaeaceae]].<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |title=nenuphar |encyclopedia=[[Chambers Dictionary]] |publisher=[[Chambers (publisher)|Chambers]] |year=2003 |isbn=0-550-10105-5 |edition=9th}}</ref><ref>{{cite Lexico|nenuphar |access-date=2022-04-01}} {{Cite web |url=https://www.lexico.com/definition/nenuphare |title=Archived copy |access-date=2025-11-02 |archive-date=2022-04-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220401155633/https://www.lexico.com/definition/nenuphare |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=minn /> It is native to [[North Africa]], temperate Asia, Europe, and tropical Asia ([[Jammu and Kashmir (union territory)|Jammu and Kashmir]]).<ref name="Grin">{{cite web |title=Taxon: Nymphaea alba L. |url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?id=25429 |access-date=2017-10-23}}</ref>

Since ''Nymphaea alba'' is an aquatic plant, its specialized trichomes are hydropotes, formed at an abaxial surface of the young leaf and packed tightly in the rosette at the rhizome's flattened apex. The rhizomes contain high amounts of carbohydrate and protein.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Kordyum|first=Elizabeth |author-link=Elizabeth Kordyum |last2=Mosyakin |first2=Sergei |last3=Ivanenko |first3=Galina |last4=Ovcharenko |first4=Yulia |last5=Brykov |first5=Vasyl |date=2021-02-01 |title=Hydropotes of young and mature leaves in Nuphar lutea and Nymphaea alba (Nymphaeaceae): Formation, functions and phylogeny |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304377020301522 |journal=[[Aquatic Botany]] |volume=169 |article-number=103342 |doi=10.1016/j.aquabot.2020.103342 |issn=0304-3770 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Description==
''Nymphaea alba'' has a round dark green leaves up to {{convert|35|cm|in|abbr=on}} in length<ref>{{cite book |last1=Mossberg |first1=Bo |last2=Stenberg |first2=Lennart |last3=Karlsson |first3=Thomas |title=Nordens flora |date=2018 |publisher=Bonnier Fakta |location=Stockholm |isbn=9789174245264 |pages=70}}</ref> and white flowers which usually bloom during the daytime in summer. Both leaves and flowers float on the water's surface. At first, the flower is cup-shaped, with a size of around {{convert|8|cm|in|abbr=on}}. It increases to {{convert|20|cm|in|abbr=on}} and becomes star-shaped over time. The flower's petals are arranged in a row, pointing up surrounding many yellow stamens.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nymphaea alba (White Water Lily) |url=https://www.gardenia.net/plant/nymphaea-alba |website=www.gardenia.net}}</ref><ref name=vit>{{cite web|last1=Anderberg|first1=Anders|title=Vit näckros|url=http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/di/nymphaea/nymph/nympalb.html|website=www.linnaeus.nrm.se|publisher=[[Swedish Museum of Natural History]]|access-date=18 August 2015|date=1996|language=sv}}</ref> The species may spread {{convert|150|cm|in|abbr=on}} per plant.<ref name=minn>{{cite web |title=Nymphaea alba (H) |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/11623/nymphaea-alba-h/details |website=RHS |access-date=29 August 2026}}</ref>

==Cytology==
The chromosome count is n = 42. The genome size is 1950 Mb.<ref name = "Chen et al., 2017">{{cite journal | url=https://academic.oup.com/hr/article-pdf/doi/10.1038/hortres.2017.51/41958119/41438_2017_article_bfhortres201751.pdf | doi=10.1038/hortres.2017.51 | title=Water lilies as emerging models for Darwin's abominable mystery | year=2017 | last1=Chen | first1=Fei | last2=Liu | first2=Xing | last3=Yu | first3=Cuiwei | last4=Chen | first4=Yuchu | last5=Tang | first5=Haibao | last6=Zhang | first6=Liangsheng | journal=Horticulture Research | volume=4 | page=17051 | pmid=28979789 | pmc=5626932 }}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
It was first published and described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his book '[[Species Plantarum]]', on page 510 in 1753.<ref name="Grin"/><ref>{{cite web|title=Nymphaeaceae Nymphaea alba L.|url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=171158-2|publisher=.pni.org|access-date=23 October 2017}}</ref> It is the type species of its genus.<ref name = "Tropicos a">Missouri Botanical Garden. (n.d.-af). ''Nymphaea'' L. Tropicos. Retrieved March 3, 2025, from https://www.tropicos.org/name/40029644</ref> Within the subgenus [[Nymphaea subg. Nymphaea|''Nymphaea'' subg. ''Nymphaea'']] it is placed in the section [[Nymphaea sect. Nymphaea|''Nymphaea'' sect. ''Nymphaea'']].<ref name="Grin"/>

The red variety (''Nymphaea alba'' f. ''rosea'') is cultivated from lake [[Fagertärn]] ("Fair tarn") in the forest of [[Tiveden]], Sweden, where it was discovered in the early 19th century. The  discovery led to large-scale exploitation which nearly made it extinct in the wild before it was protected.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Wallsten|first1=Maud|last2=Thorson|first2=Jan|last3=Werlemark|first3=Gun|journal=[[Svensk Botanisk Tidskrift]]|date=2005|issue=99:3–4|title=Härstammar Claude Monets röda näckrosor från Fagertärn i Närke?|trans-title=Are Claude Monet's red water lilies derived from Fagertärn in Närke?|pages=146–153|url=http://sbf.c.se/www/pdf/99(3-4)/Wallsten.pdf|access-date=18 August 2015|language=sv|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304063741/http://sbf.c.se/www/pdf/99%283-4%29/Wallsten.pdf|archive-date=4 March 2016}}</ref>

''[[Nymphaea candida]]'' {{small|J. Presl}} is sometimes considered a [[subspecies]] of ''N. alba'' (''N. alba'' L. subsp. ''candida'' {{small|(J. Presl) Korsh.}}).<ref name=vit />

==Distribution and habitat==
''Nymphaea alba'' is [[Native species|native]] all over Europe and in parts of North Africa and the Middle East in fresh water.<ref name = "POWO, 2024 a"/><ref name=vit/> In Africa, it is found in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia. In temperate Asia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Siberia, Iran, Iraq, Palestine and Turkey. It is found in tropical Asia, within the Indian territory of Jammu and Kashmir. Lastly, within Europe, it is found in Belarus, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Moldova, Russian Federation, Ukraine, Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, Germany, Hungary, Netherlands, Poland, Slovakia, Switzerland, Denmark, Finland, Ireland, Norway, Sweden, United Kingdom, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Italy, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Romania, Serbia, Slovenia, France, Portugal and Spain.<ref name="Grin"/> It has been introduced to the Azores, Bangladesh, Chile, parts of China, Myanmar, and New Zealand.<ref name = "POWO, 2024 a"/>

''Nymphaea alba'' grows in ponds, ditches, lakes, or canals with still or slow-moving water.<ref>{{Cite web |title=White water-lily {{!}} The Wildlife Trusts |url=https://www.wildlifetrusts.org/wildlife-explorer/wildflowers/white-water-lily |access-date=2024-11-19 |website=www.wildlifetrusts.org |language=en}}</ref>

==Phytochemistry==
It contains the active [[alkaloid]]s [[nupharine]] and [[nymphaeine]], and is a sedative and an aphrodisiac/anaphrodisiac depending on sources.{{citation needed|date=September 2016}} Although roots and stalks are used in traditional herbal medicine along with the flower, the petals and other flower parts are the most potent. Alcohol can be used to extract the active alkaloids, and it also boosts the sedative effects. The root of the plant was used by monks and nuns for hundreds of years as an [[anaphrodisiac]], being crushed and mixed with wine. In the earliest printed medical textbooks, authors  maintained this use, though warning against consuming large and frequent doses.<ref name=gift>{{cite book|last1=Nielsen|title=Giftplanter|trans-title=Poisonous plants|date=1979|publisher=[[J.W. Cappelens Forlag|Cappelen]]|isbn=87-01-31841-1|pages=68–69|series=Gyldendals grønne håndbøger|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wiBoRAAACAAJ|language=no}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
''Nymphaea alba'' is a vigorous plant which needs plenty of space as the leaves can spread up to {{convert|1.5|m|ft|abbr=on}}. It prefers to grow in clay or loam in full sun. When it is first introduced into the water, it should be placed rather shallow with the rhizome at around {{convert|20|cm|in|abbr=on}} below the surface.
As the plant gets established it can be sunk deeper down to a depth of about 90 cm. In nature it regularly grows deeper than this.<ref>{{cite web |title=Nymphaea alba (H) {{!}} white waterlily |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/11623/nymphaea-alba-h/details |website=RHS |access-date=29 August 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

In north-eastern [[India]] young leaves and peduncles of ''Nymphaea alba'' and other species are harvested and eaten as vegetables. The rhizomes are also harvested to be boiled and eaten. Parts of the plant have been used as [[traditional medicine]] to treat diarrhea, piles, coughing and other ailments.
The flowers are also harvested for decoration and for their pleasant smell, and have a long vase-life.
